questions.question: Q: What is virtus and how does its meaning differ between Caesar and Cicero?
questions.correctAnswer: Virtus means manly courage or excellence. In Caesar, it primarily means military bravery and leadership. In Cicero, it extends to moral courage — the determination to defend the Republic and speak the truth against threats like Catiline.

questions.question: Q: How does Caesar portray the Gauls in De Bello Gallico?
questions.correctAnswer: Caesar portrays Gauls as fierce and warlike but also disorganised and culturally inferior to Romans. However, he admires certain Gallic leaders like Vercingetorix for their courage. His portrayal serves his purpose: exaggerating the Gallic threat justifies his conquest.

questions.question: Q: What is pietas and why is it important in Roman culture?
questions.correctAnswer: Pietas is duty and devotion to the gods, one's country, and one's family. It is a core Roman value that governs behaviour: Aeneas embodies pietas by putting duty to his mission above personal desire. Conflicts arise when different pietas obligations clash.

tests.name: Exam-Style Practice
tests.description: Short-answer practice on Themes in Prose Literature

questions.question: Q: How does Tacitus explore the theme of libertas vs tyranny?
questions.correctAnswer: Tacitus shows how the principate destroyed Republican libertas: senators are reduced to flattering the emperor, free speech is punished, and genuine political opposition is eliminated. His history mourns the loss of freedom under emperors like Tiberius.

questions.question: Q: What is the mos maiorum and why does it matter in Latin literature?
questions.correctAnswer: The mos maiorum (customs of the ancestors) is the unwritten code of traditional Roman behaviour and values. Characters in set texts are judged against it: those who follow it are praised, and those who abandon it are condemned.

questions.question: Q: How does Cicero present himself in the Catilinarians?
questions.correctAnswer: Cicero presents himself as the saviour of the Republic, a consul who through courage and intelligence exposed and defeated the Catilinarian conspiracy. He emphasises his own virtus and the Senate's gratitude, using the speeches to boost his political standing.

questions.question: Q: What role does fear play in Caesar's narrative?
questions.correctAnswer: Caesar uses fear both as a theme and a tool: fear of Gallic uprisings justifies his campaigns; fear among his own troops tests their disciplina; and he uses fear to control enemies through ruthless demonstrations of Roman power.

questions.question: Q: How do Roman authors use the concept of barbarism?
questions.correctAnswer: Romans use 'barbarus' to define their own civilised identity against foreign 'others'. Caesar describes barbarian customs (druidic sacrifice, polygamy) as evidence of Roman superiority. However, Tacitus in the Germania suggests Germanic simplicity may be morally superior to Roman corruption.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response Discuss how the themes of leadership and imperialism are presented in Latin prose literature, referring to specific set text authors. (8 marks) <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Leadership and imperialism are central themes in Latin prose literature, but different authors present them very differently. Caesar presents leadership as the exercise of personal virtus and decisive action. In De Bello Gallico, he portrays himself as the ideal leader: calm in crisis (as in the Nervii battle), resourceful, and always present at the front. His leadership justifies Roman imperialism: the conquest of Gaul is presented as necessary to protect Rome from barbarian threats and to bring civilisation to backward peoples. The Gallic tribes are shown as fierce but disorganised, needing Roman order. However, Caesar's self-portrait is propaganda: his narrative deliberately enhances his dignitas and political standing back in Rome. Cicero presents a different model of leadership: not military but political and moral. In the Catilinarians, his leadership is oratorical and intellectual — he saves the Republic through rhetoric and political wisdom, not swords. His imperialism is defensive: he seeks to protect Roman libertas from internal enemies who would destroy the Republic from within. Tacitus offers the most critical perspective on both themes. His portraits of emperors in the Annales show how imperial leadership can degenerate into tyranny: Tiberius's hypocrisy, Sejanus's treachery, and the Senate's cowardly acquiescence all demonstrate how the principate corrupts leadership.
